beliefs.limiting: I’ve smoked for years. I’m stuck.
beliefs.counterpart: Most people hooked on weed get free in the end.
beliefs.test: This week, list the people you know who smoked every day for years and don’t now. Ask one how long he smoked before he stopped. Notice how many years most of them had behind them.
beliefs.proof: In a US survey, 344 of 530 adults ever hooked on weed were already free when asked; half are projected to get free about 6 years after first getting hooked. “Free” means no signs of being hooked, not never smoking.

refs.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction 106(3):657-69. Table 3 (Table 1 gives cannabis dependence N=530).

Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Addiction 106(3):657-69.
refs.quote: Half of cannabis dependence remissions occurred approximately 6 years after dependence onset among Whites and Blacks, 5 years among Hispanics and NH/PI and 7 years among AI/AN

beliefs.origin: 06-template.json cannabis belief 5. Limiting kept. Counterpart put in the form of the row marked Keep (RULEBOOK rule 22): the old “97% … I’m next” rested on a lifetime projection and read as a slogan; the proof now leads with the counted 344 of 530 (rule 10).

problems: The 6-year figure is a projection. The paper says 'These projections were obtained by the standard actuarial method', built from ages people recalled. The proof says 'an estimated half', but rule 10 needs the word 'projected' or 'expected'.

Open doubt, no change made: the paper never says in words that 344 of the 530 had remitted by the interview. 344 is only the column header 'Cannabis remission (N=344)' in Tables 3 and 4 (the survival analyses). Reading it as the number who remitted fits the 66.2% remitted a decade after onset, but it is an inference.

Checked and holds: 530 adults had lifetime DSM-IV cannabis dependence (NESARC, US, 2001–2002, n=43,093). Remission means they 'finally stopped having any of these experiences (dependence criteria)', not that they stopped using, so the 'Free' line is right. Severity 'dependent' fits. Both quotes are word for word: 3 and 27 words. The fixed proof is 39 words.

beliefs.limiting: I can’t handle quitting. Last time I barely lasted three days.
beliefs.counterpart: It’s a few hard weeks, not forever. I’ve got through hard weeks before.
beliefs.test: Tonight, wait an hour before your first smoke. Rate the urge 0 to 10 every 10 minutes. Notice whether it keeps climbing or comes in waves you can sit through.
beliefs.proof: Weed withdrawal usually lasts up to 3 weeks; poor sleep can last longer. In 49 people hooked on weed and paid to stay off, the harm to daily life over two weeks was on average fairly mild.

refs.cite: Bonnet U, Preuss UW (2017). The cannabis withdrawal syndrome: current insights. Substance Abuse and Rehabilitation 8:9-37.
refs.quote: The CWS usually lasts up to 3 weeks

refs.cite: Connor JP, Stjepanović D, Budney AJ, Le Foll B, Hall WD (2022). Clinical management of cannabis withdrawal. Addiction 117(7):2075-2095.
refs.quote: Sleep disturbances may continue for several weeks or longer.

refs.cite: Allsop DJ, Copeland J, Norberg MM, Fu S, Molnar A, Lewis J, Budney AJ (2012). Quantifying the clinical significance of cannabis withdrawal. PLoS One 7(9):e44864. 49 non-treatment-seeking users in Sydney who met DSM-IV criteria for dependence; two weeks of monitored abstinence with a one-hour psychological session and contingency payments up to AU$450.
refs.quote: It is of note that the average level of functional impairment caused by cannabis withdrawal symptoms was relatively mild

problems: 'Not in treatment' reads more hopeful than the study. The 49 were not seeking treatment, but the study gave them support to stay off: 'The cannabis abstinence attempt was supported with a one-hour psychological intervention and contingency management payments totalling AU$450 for adherence to study protocol'. A reader who tries alone gets neither.

The 'relatively mild' line comes from the discussion. The paper's conclusion is that withdrawal 'is clinically significant because it is associated with functional impairment to normal daily activities, as well as relapse'. Harm was greater in the most hooked (p=0.03). The fix keeps the authors' own 'on average' line but names the payment. There is no room under 40 words for the 'worse for the most hooked' clause.

Checked and holds: Bonnet 2017 says 'The CWS usually lasts up to 3 weeks' and Connor 2022 says 'Sleep disturbances may continue for several weeks or longer.' Allsop has n=49 who met DSM-IV dependence criteria, Sydney, Australia, two weeks of monitored abstinence. Severity 'dependent' fits, and all three quotes are word for word.

beliefs.limiting: Day 10, I feel fine. Now I can handle it.
beliefs.counterpart: Feeling fine means the withdrawal is over, not that I’m in control again.
beliefs.test: Write down every time you said “just one”, “only weekends” or “just a break”. Next to each, write how long it took to be back to daily. Notice the pattern.
beliefs.proof: Of 82 people treated for weed dependence who got 2+ weeks off, 71% smoked again within 6 months, and 71% of those went back to 4+ days a week. Early slips led back more often.

refs.cite: Moore BA, Budney AJ (2003). Relapse in outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment 25(2):85-9.
refs.quote: Seventy-one percent used marijuana at least once (i.e., lapsed) within 6 months of initial abstinence, averaging 73 days (SD = 50) till lapsing.

refs.cite: Moore BA, Budney AJ (2003). Relapse in outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment 25(2):85-9.
refs.quote: Similarly, 71% of those who lapsed, relapsed to heavier use defined as at least 4 days of marijuana use in any 7-day period.

refs.cite: Moore BA, Budney AJ (2003). Relapse in outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment 25(2):85-9.
refs.quote: Early lapses were more strongly associated with consequent relapse.

beliefs.origin: 06-template.json cannabis belief 4. Limiting and counterpart kept word for word. Proof replaced: the old one rested on quitters’ stories and a receptor finding; rule 4 needs a study of people who had been hooked.

problems: Only the abstract is open; the full text is paywalled. Every claim is in the abstract: 82 people with 2 or more weeks off during outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence; 71% lapsed within 6 months; 71% of those who lapsed relapsed to 4 or more days in any 7-day period; early lapses were more strongly tied to relapse.

Rule 4 holds: the sample is people treated for dependence, tagged 'treatment', not 'heavy' or 'users'. Proof is 35 words. All three quotes are word for word (23, 23 and 9 words). No other drug is named.

beliefs.limiting: Weed is the only thing that gets me to sleep.
beliefs.counterpart: Weed knocks me out. It doesn’t give me good sleep. Some rough weeks buy my real sleep back.
beliefs.test: For 7 mornings, rate how rested you feel, 0 to 10, and note whether you remember a dream. Notice whether being knocked out is the same as waking up rested.
beliefs.proof: Of 302 adults hooked on weed starting a treatment trial, 69% slept poorly at the start. Over 12 weeks, sleep improved more for those who cut down than for those whose use rose.

refs.cite: Hser YI, Mooney LJ, Huang D, Zhu Y, Tomko RL, McClure E, et al. (2017). Reductions in cannabis use are associated with improvements in anxiety, depression, and sleep quality, but not quality of life. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment 81:53-58. 302 adults with DSM-IV cannabis dependence in the ACCENT trial.
refs.quote: A high percentage (68.9%) of the study sample reported poor sleep quality.

beliefs.origin: 06-template.json cannabis belief 2. Limiting kept. Counterpart: “A few rough nights” changed to “Some rough weeks” to fix a fact (sleep trouble can last several weeks or longer). Proof replaced: the old one counted users and inpatients not checked for dependence.

problems: 'Those who cut down slept better than those whose use rose' overstates the result. The paper compared change over time (the slope of sleep scores, β=-0.07, p<0.05), not sleep levels at the end. At baseline the reduction group's PSQI was 6.5 against 6.3. The source says the people who cut down had 'improvements of sleep quality over time' compared with the others.
This is an association, not proof that cutting down caused better sleep. Everyone was also in a trial with contingency management. Not in the proof text; noted for the 'what is weak' list.

Checked and holds: 302 adults with DSM-IV cannabis dependence (ACCENT, US multisite, 12 weeks). 208 of 302 (68.9%) had poor sleep at baseline (PSQI above 5). The groups were 152 cut down and 150 rose. Severity 'dependent' fits, and both quotes are word for word.

do: Write down what weed does for you: sleep, boredom, anxiety, fun.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Keep smoking as usual for a few days while you do this. No cutting down yet.
Before each smoke, note the time, where you are and what you want from it.
After it, note whether it gave you that, and for how long.
Allow it. No guilt while you log: you’re investigating, not failing.
Sleep: same wake-up time every day, no screens in bed.
Evenings: plan the first 14 in advance: gym, cooking, a friend, a game.
Anxiety: a walk or a hard workout when it spikes.
Boredom: two things that keep your hands busy, set up before the date.
Keep the ritual, swap the joint: same break, same balcony, tea or a walk instead.
For each need on your step 1 list, write one swap. 80% of the effect is enough.

proof.text: Of 25 long-time daily smokers who quit without treatment for a year or more, the most common things that kept them off were avoiding situations where they smoked, a changed routine and new interests. A small group.

ref.cite: Ellingstad TP, Sobell LC, Sobell MB, Eickleberry L, Golden CJ (2006). Self-change: a pathway to cannabis abuse resolution. Addictive Behaviors 31(3):519-30.
ref.quote: The most common reported maintenance factors were avoidance of situations in which cannabis was used, changes in lifestyle, and the development of non-cannabis-related interests.

problems: Only the abstract is open. It supports every part: 'Long-term daily cannabis abusers (N = 25) who without treatment stopped using cannabis for at least one year'; the maintenance factors as quoted; and 'A small group' names the weakness. Small and minor: 'a changed routine' stands for the source's 'changes in lifestyle'.

The quote is word for word (24 words) and the proof is 37 words. Plan proofs have no severity field. The source's group, long-term daily 'cannabis abusers', is if anything more of a problem group than the proof's wording, so the proof is not more hopeful.

do: Pick a date a few days to a few weeks out. Put it in your calendar. Smoke as usual until then.
Throw out the stash, grinder and papers. Delete the dealer’s number.
Expect the first two weeks to be the hardest.
For three months, weed is the one thing. No new diet, no new life plan.
Every day without weed is a complete success. Mark it off.
If you slip, you’re not back at zero. Go back through steps 1–3, find what the slip gave you, and set a new date.

proof.text: In 18 heavy users who stopped, symptoms usually started on days 1–3, peaked on days 2–6, and most lasted 4–14 days.

ref.cite: Budney AJ, Moore BA, Vandrey RG, Hughes JR (2003). The time course and significance of cannabis withdrawal. Journal of Abnormal Psychology 112(3):393-402.
ref.quote: Onset typically occurred between Days 1-3, peak effects between Days 2-6, and most effects lasted 4-14 days.

problems: 'Most were gone by day 14' is not what the source says. The source says 'most effects lasted 4-14 days'. That is how long the effects lasted, counted from an onset on days 1–3, so the end could fall after day 14. The proof reads more hopeful than the source.
Checked and holds: 18 marijuana users, after heavy use, a 45-day abstinence phase (Vermont, US). Peak on days 2–6 matches. The quote is word for word (17 words). Only the abstract is open.

do: When someone offers, say “I don’t smoke”, not “I’m taking a break”.
Notice the “I can moderate now” thought, and treat it as a symptom.
When the urge hits, say “there is a craving”, not “I need to smoke”. Then watch it.
Rate it 0 to 10 and watch it drop. You don’t have to fight it or obey it.
Expect “just one” once you feel fine. Decide your answer now, not at the party.
Tell the people you smoke with that you’ve stopped. Not paused: stopped.

proof.text: In a 12-week treatment trial of 302 adults hooked on weed, craving started lowest and fell within weeks for 41%, and started moderate and fell over time for another 38%. Everyone was paid for clean tests.

ref.cite: Alias-Ferri M, Flesaker M, Gray K, Tomko R, McPherson S, Korthuis PT, et al. (2026). Longitudinal craving profiles in cannabis use disorder: a latent class growth analysis of the ACCENT (CTN-0053) trial. Drug and Alcohol Dependence 285:113208.
ref.quote: A four-class solution provided the best fit: low craving (41%), moderate-decreasing craving (38%), moderate-stable craving (11%), and high craving (10%).

problems: 'Craving stayed low for 41%' is wrong. The full text says the low class 'had the lowest mean baseline craving (M = 38.6). Craving then declined through three weeks after randomization before leveling off at week 4 (M = 16.0).' It started lowest and fell; it did not stay flat.
All participants got contingency management (paid for clean urine tests) on top of NAC or placebo. A reader quitting alone does not get this, so the fix says so.

Checked and holds: N=302 adults who met DSM-IV cannabis dependence (CTN-0053 ACCENT, US multisite, 12 weeks plus a week-17 follow-up). The classes were 123 (41%) and 116 (38%) of 302. The quote is word for word (20 words). The fixed proof is 36 words.

do: Look for CBT with motivation sessions, over a month or more.
Ask about programmes that reward clean tests.
Help is a tool, not a verdict. Use what works, drop what doesn’t.
Free and quick: one friend who quit, an online quit group, a Marijuana Anonymous meeting.
A few meetings can be enough. You don’t sign up for life.

proof.text: In 6 trials with 1,166 people with a weed problem, therapy made people about 2.5 times as likely to be off weed at about 4 months as little or no treatment. Low-quality evidence.

ref.cite: Gates PJ, Sabioni P, Copeland J, Le Foll B, Gowing L (2016). Psychosocial interventions for cannabis use disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2016(5):CD005336.
ref.quote: low-quality evidence revealed that those receiving intervention were more likely to report point-prevalence abstinence (risk ratio (RR) 2.55, 95% CI 1.34 to 4.83, six studies, 1166 participants)

problems: Every part is in the abstract: RR 2.55 (95% CI 1.34 to 4.83) for self-reported point-prevalence abstinence; 6 studies and 1,166 participants; intervention against inactive control at early follow-up (median 4 months); rated low quality. The quote is word for word (27 words) and the proof is 33 words. 'A weed problem' fits 'cannabis use disorder'.

Context, not an error: the interval is wide (1.34 to 4.83). The review also says 'approximately one-quarter of participants abstinent at final follow-up' and that no intervention was consistently effective at 9 months or later. The proof's 'at about 4 months' and 'Low-quality evidence' keep it from overclaiming.

notUsed.reason: The reader already knows he is hooked (rule 1); answering this reads as screening him. Its proof counts all past-year users (3 in 10) and regular users (47%), not people hooked (rules 2–3). The 47% stays in 07-mirror-stats.

Its proof (4.8 times the odds of psychosis) counts daily strong-weed users not checked for addiction (heavy). It argues for quitting, which the reader already wants; it does not answer a thought that stops him. The number stays in 07-mirror-stats.
